0c90ca142bf46693: ROME: Security forces are deploying in large numbers across Italy on Saturday for protests planned in eight cities, including Rome and Milan, after some demonstrations turned violent last weekend.
The demonstrations come amid a wave of protests by students, truck drivers and farmers over budget cuts and cost-of-living issues such as housing and fuel prices.
Rome's police force said in a statement it would "saturate both physical and virtual territory" and use drones and helicopters to monitor the demonstrations.
It said it still "aimed to safeguard the full exercise of the right to express one's views, including dissent, but strictly in compliance with the law".
In Milan, extra soldiers deployed following last weekend's protests will patrol the city centre, but Mayor Giuseppe Sala said there were no plans to shut down the city.
"Last weekend there weren't enough of us. We will simply try to be more numerous," he told Radio Lombardia.
Sala also encouraged shops to remain open on Saturday, after several boutiques in the fashion hub were looted last weekend and others closed or removed their window displays.
"If panic spreads then everything stops," he said on Friday.
A group calling itself the "Oct 17 Movement" has called for protests at 1300 GMT in eight Italian cities.
It said there would be three protests in each city, which would converge at one location, and that the locations would only be revealed half an hour before the start.
Separately, an anti-war movement called the "Anti-imperialist Axis" has also organised a rally in Rome.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's hard-right government adopted a security decree this week that eases detention rules for minors, introduces an offence of "violent participation in a demonstration" and imposes fines on parents for damage caused by their children during protests.
Police said on Friday they had carried out dozens of raids against people suspected of taking part in looting and rioting during last weekend's protests.
The government has also approved a series of measures to help truck drivers and fishermen cope with the spike in fuel prices.
Almost all the truck blockades that had paralysed southern Italy, causing fuel and food shortages for days, have now been lifted.
0e81e9c236a7c5aa: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had ordered a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to prevent certification of Alaska's Senate election result if the Republican incumbent loses — raising further questions over whether he will accept defeat in the midterms.

"I'm the one that said, 'Do it,'" Trump announced during a trip to Florida, where he is due to cast his own early ballot for the November 3 election to decide control of Congress, currently in Republican hands.
The extraordinary intervention by a president to launch a pre-emptive challenge to a possible election result casts a new shadow over the midterms.

Trump — who tried to overturn the 2020 presidential election after losing to Democrat Joe Biden — has repeatedly questioned the validity of the upcoming election, in which Democrats are forecast to make big gains.

If Democrats win the House of Representatives, as widely expected, they would be able to exert the first real brake on Trump's unprecedented exercise of power since he secured his second term two years ago.

Democrats also have an outside chance of winning the Senate if they can flip a handful of Republican-held seats, including in Alaska, where incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola.
She called the lawsuit "corruption" in a post on X.
Sullivan v Sullivan

In its lawsuit, filed on Thursday, the Justice Department alleged that the presence on the Alaska ballot of a minor additional candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. was part of a deliberate ploy to confuse voters and harm the Republican incumbent's chances.
"The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan," the lawsuit said.
Democrats and Sullivan Jr. himself, a registered Republican, have denied this.
The lawsuit asks for certification of a Democratic win to be held up pending an investigation if the Republican incumbent's losing margin is smaller than the number of votes won by his namesake.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has repeatedly broken Washington norms about maintaining political distance from the White House, said on Thursday that the Justice Department was not preparing to interfere in the midterms.
But he refused to rule out what he called a "doomsday scenario".
"To say that there's no circumstances that we would ever do that. Of course, I'm not going to say that."

Democrats have accused the Trump administration of seeking ways to steer the results of the November vote by trying to expand federal government control over state-run elections and repeatedly questioning the integrity of results.

Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in his 2024 comeback election. But amid growing discontent with Republicans and Trump nationwide, Peltola, a former tribal judge and Alaska Native, is running a strong race.
Alaska is a vast state with a population of just 740,000.
Legal analyst Derek Muller described the Department of Justice's case as "absurdly thin" and unlikely to prevail in court.
"There's essentially no likelihood of success," Muller wrote on the Election Law Blog.
Sullivan Jr. was briefly removed from the ballot this summer but was reinstated by an Alaskan lower court — a decision upheld by the state's supreme court.

b32cf3fef29210b8: GENEVA: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine during the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began on Friday, the head of the World Health Organisation said.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.

Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will undergo a full-scale human trial in the DRC to determine whether it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.

"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work.
"In the meantime, the existing Everbo vaccine (licensed for use in preventing other Ebola virus disease) will be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."

The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC — a single trial framework that can test the safety and efficacy of multiple vaccines — should eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are undergoing earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.

600ae33278f6dbdc: NEW YORK: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a US Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Friday.
Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street.

"There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. "There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34.

Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.
Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.

American Express shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce.
SLB shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting. Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio.

34ab135f286c57f6: HEBRON: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major military operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in an attack near Hebron, days ahead of Israeli elections in which security has been a central focus.

Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday's vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe, and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the attack to pledge an even harder line on West Bank militancy.

The first steps would see Hebron residents displaced, homes searched and "terrorist infrastructure" destroyed, the premier said, threatening operations on a scale unseen since Israel captured the Palestinian territory in 1967.
Rebel group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised the attack as a "heroic operation" and called on supporters to carry out more.

A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between soldiers and two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle, with Israeli forces eventually shooting the attackers dead.
The army later said that two of its soldiers "fell in combat in the Judea Junction" area, with three others wounded.
Netanyahu in a statement lauded the soldiers' response, crediting them with having "prevented what could have been a major attack" and ordering a lockdown in the West Bank.

Visiting Hebron later in the day, the premier said he and defence minister Israel Katz were "considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since" the 1967 war.
"The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way," he added.
The first step would see Israeli forces "enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure".

He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, the scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the UN said forcibly displaced thousands.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from "plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes".
UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres through a spokesman voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides.
'Exactly like in Gaza'
The military said it had "launched offensive counter-terrorism operations in the Hebron area", adding that troops were raiding homes of the suspects and others.
Far-right Israeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, later announced that building demolitions were underway.
In a video from the area, he said authorities were "sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: if you mess with the Jews, you will pay a very painful price."
Earlier in the day he had called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza".
"In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply."
Also visiting the scene, National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based "Palestinian Authority must be dismantled".
"It is impossible for there to be an authority within Judea and Samaria that incites murder, calls for murder, and works for murder," he told reporters.
No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, was connected to Friday's attack.
Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal champions of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu's government but are illegal under international law.
Hamas praises attack

Hamas, which carried out the Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war, hailed Friday's shooting as a "natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people".
Netanyahu vowed to "pursue Hamas terrorists" everywhere, adding: "You have no place to hide."

Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu's top rival in the upcoming vote, likewise praised the response by troops, and said he was praying "for the complete and quick recovery of the injured".
The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters.

According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.
Israeli figures show at least 51 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.
8745462db1b68709: MOSCOW: Talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are planned to resume in November in the UAE, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Friday.

Russia indicated its readiness to resume the talks, which have been at a standstill since the beginning of the year, following a meeting this week in Saint Petersburg between President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

The next round of talks towards ending the Ukraine war, which is grinding through its fifth year, are "planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi", and "will take place in a trilateral format", Peskov told reporters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the plan to meet in November in a post on X.
"Now we all need to focus on making these meetings happen –- together with America, Europe, and all our partners," he said Friday.

The announcement came amid intensified diplomatic efforts by US President Donald Trump's administration. Witkoff met on Tuesday with Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo, before meeting with Putin on Wednesday.
Following the meetings, both Kyiv and Moscow voiced their readiness to resume direct talks mediated by Washington.

Russia, which launched its full-scale offensive against Ukraine in February 2022, has suggested talks could take place "around November 10". Zelensky has called for the discussions to happen "as soon as possible".
In a televised interview aired late Thursday, Putin said that any trilateral talks would focus on the security arrangements of a final peace deal and not a "short" truce.
eab741b272d8402b: AUSTIN: Charles Leclerc topped the times for Ferrari ahead of Red Bull’s four-time champion Max Verstappen, as Mercedes’ championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth, in Friday’s opening practice at this weekend’s United States Grand Prix.
Antonelli could clinch the drivers’ title this weekend if he wins and other drivers are unable to stay within reach of his points total.

Father-to-be Leclerc clocked a best lap time of one minute and 36.052 seconds to beat Verstappen, winner of the last two races, by 0.084 seconds with world champion Lando Norris third for McLaren, adrift by two-tenths.
George Russell, who is 102 points behind Antonelli in the drivers’ title race, was fourth for Mercedes, ahead of the 20-year-old Italian, with seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton sixth for Ferrari.
Oscar Piastri was seventh in the second McLaren ahead of Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, Racing Bulls’ rookie Arvid Lindblad, who has a five-place grid penalty, and his team-mate Liam Lawson.

The session began with a big crowd basking in warm sunshine and several teams sporting their final upgrade packages, including Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes, but the focus was on Antonelli and his title bid.

Without a win in three races since the Spanish Grand Prix, he requires a victory on Sunday and disappointing results for Russell and Hamilton, below eighth and fourth respectively, to become the youngest champion and Italy’s first since Alberto Ascari, for Ferrari, in 1953.

Haas, one of two American teams on the grid, were among the early runners on track with a special livery for their home event and following news that Brazilian driver Rafael Camara is set to join, as a probable replacement for Esteban Ocon, in 2027.
Cadillac, the second home team in their debut season, also had an upgrades package in a bid to escape the back row seats, and showed potential in the early stages with Valtteri Bottas up to 16th.

By then, Verstappen’s preliminary fastest lap on hard tyres had been overhauled by Leclerc on mediums. The Monegasque driver, whose wife Alexandra Saint Mleux, is expecting their first child, appeared to be in the mood as he clocked 1:36.761 ahead of team-mate Hamilton by 0.074.

Leclerc switched to softs after half an hour and trimmed his lap to 1:36.052, enough to resist a rapid Verstappen lap on softs by 0.084 with Norris third ahead of Antonelli and Hamilton, who survived a slide at Turn One. Russell was sixth.
The track, declared as unacceptably bumpy by Verstappen and Norris, was clearly ‘rubbering in’ as Verstappen went top before the lap was scratched for exceeding track limits.
It was proof nonetheless that he was in the mix and ahead of both Mercedes – a position that makes it unlikely Antonelli will find it easy to achieve his goal this Sunday.

ab9b549ba929ad31: BERLIN: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital by an emergency medical team on Friday after collapsing during training, the club said.
"Vincent Kompany had to seek medical attention on Friday after collapsing during a training session with FC Bayern's reserve team," Bayern said on their website.
"Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations at the hospital and will remain under medical care."
Kompany, the 40-year-old former Manchester City defender, missed training and a press conference on Tuesday ahead of Bayern's Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena.

"We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure he recovers quickly. Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, as well as all the time he needs. His coaching staff, whom we trust completely, will take over his duties."
English assistant coach Aaron Danks took training and handled the press conference ahead of the Arsenal game.
"It affected his legs at times; he was experiencing some pain. It's just a virus. He needs rest," Danks said on Tuesday.
"The most important thing we're encouraging him to do right now is to rest and take as much time as he needs—no matter how long that may be."
Bundesliga leaders Bayern visit Freiburg, who are third in the table, on Saturday.
Their next Champions League match is on Nov 3 in Madrid against Atletico.
The Spanish club posted their best wishes on social media.
"We wish you a speedy recovery. We hope to see you here in Madrid, on the bench, in a few days," wrote the Spanish club adding a heart emoji.
'Friendly and approachable'

Kompany, a centreback, started his career with Anderlecht in his native Brussels. He moved to Hamburg and then to Manchester City as one of the club's last signings before the Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
He went on to play 360 games for the club, where he was also captain for eight season as the team became the dominant force in English football.
He played 89 times for Belgium and finished his playing career back at Anderlecht in 2019 where he was player-coach in the first of his three seasons in charge
He took over at Burnley in 2022, leading them to a Championship title in 2023 but the club was relegated the next season with their lowest ever points total.
Bayern, who had just endured a trophyless season and had been unable to persuade Thomas Tuchel to stay, sprung a surprise by paying Burnley to sign Kompany as manager in 2024.

He led the club two the Bundesliga title each of his first two seasons and to a German Cup in 2026. After six games, Bayern lead the table this season on goal difference. In 74 Bundesliga games under Kompany, Bayern have won 57 and lost three.
Kompany completed an MBA at Manchester Business School in 2018.
"The way Vinnie combines coaching ability with personal qualities is extraordinary," Eberl said recently.
"He is always friendly, open, and approachable. Yet, he knows exactly what he wants and how he wants it done on the pitch,"
c636a8319993faee: Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.  “It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.  Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.  “Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.   Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.  “It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.  A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.  In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.  “As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”  That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking. “Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said. To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”  Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus. MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954. “He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”  She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”  Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”  Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University. Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).  In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.  Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”  For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.  “We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.  Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.  “I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.” She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

129661734740ec73: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems. But this one won’t receive an emergency fix.

The PHP Foundation on Friday told The Register that it has reserved a CVE identifier (CVE-2026-115560) for a third RCE flaw to go with the first two that comprise PHP2Shell, and it will release a full advisory and fixed software with the next regular PHP release.

CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”
The informational advisory, published on Friday, suggests that users “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled.

This setup, according to the PHP Foundation, is unlikely in real-world applications, and as such doesn’t pose the same massive risk as the earlier two CVEs that set the internet on fire earlier this week.

Those, of course, are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell. The related vulnerabilities involve memory-safety flaws in PHP, the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites with a known server-side programming language. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and patched both bugs on Wednesday.

Despite reports of mass exploitation attempts, and multiple proof-of-concept exploits both before and after the CVE disclosures, as of Friday there have been no publicly confirmed successful compromises attributed to PHP2Shell.

“We have no evidence of successful exploitation of the two vulnerabilities from Wednesday prior to disclosure, and we currently have no evidence of any exploitation of these vulnerabilities on patched PHP versions,” Barron said. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems.”
The Register reached out to multiple other security researchers, all of whom said they’ve documented exploitation attempts - but no confirmed successful attacks in the wild.

“Nonetheless, exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious,” Mandiant Chief Technology Officer Charles Carmakal said in a Friday LinkedIn post. Google Cloud owns Mandiant, along with cloud security biz Wiz, which is one of the organizations credited with finding and reporting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.
Despite “no evidence of successful wide scale exploitation,” Carmakal noted that there are several exploit PoCs publicly circulating online.

Many of these, he said, “appear to be ‘vibe-coded’ and are incapable of remote code execution. We have validated some PoCs, however, that are capable of RCE against default deployments of mod_php but not PHP-FPM.”®

60c7eb065c480fbc: At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society. The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.  “How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth. The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching. Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence. “AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.” In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024. “Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.” Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching. “MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science. Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone. “Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.” Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond  Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions. “We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee. The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students. Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching. “MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.” Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught. “I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said. During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans. “We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines.  “What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said. Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.”  “If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle. Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society. “I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.” Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future  The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production). “Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary. Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.” On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences. Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work. “SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said. Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health). “This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.” During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied.  “There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?” Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example. Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.” “A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said. As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event. “I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

91f14105229e4df6: An independent evaluation of OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system revealed that the system was not fit for purpose during a period when the company's bots were breaking into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. The safeguards weren't nearly strong enough.

"The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st," said evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research in a report released on Thursday.

The system, since improved according to OpenAI, was intended to monitor AI agent behavior. But as described by METR and Redwood Research, its monitoring capability was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor.

Bypassing the system wasn't always necessary because it wasn't always operative. Monitoring was suspended, for example, during compaction events. Compaction is a process by which AI models condense the data in their context window to make room for further input. And between May and July 2026, about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report.

That gap was theoretically large enough to allow AI agents to postpone monitoring indefinitely: agents could further suppress monitoring by continuing to take actions without returning control to the user.

"At the time of the exercise, the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions," the report explains.

This is not to say that OpenAI agents necessarily did so – the actions they did take, against Hugging Face and other organizations, have now been well documented. But OpenAI's internal monitoring system could easily have missed any misbehavior, were the company's AI agents inclined to conceal their activities – by acting during compaction – or simply to operate in system blind spots.
The report continues in this vein, citing not only monitoring gaps but poorly constructed software – dare we say vibe-coded? – that gave OpenAI agents the means to evade the shoddy monitoring.

"We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," the report says. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored."

The details of this exploit were redacted by OpenAI, but to summarize: the monitoring system that missed some traffic could be avoided by agents that were constrained by a non-working sandbox and had access to an exploit to evade monitoring.

But that's not all. The evaluators found that AI agents could craft inputs that caused monitoring to fail, that there were two client-controllable headers capable of disabling the monitoring of new agents, and that there were two unmonitored agentic tools that were thought to be read-only but could be exploited to take arbitrary action in the sandbox – which as noted above leaked like a sieve.

In conclusion, METR and Redwood Research propose that the agent monitoring systems used by AI companies actually work and are robust enough to "withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale." ®

347637be1578cbcf: Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.
But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.
“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”

d662b491c832d00b: SINGAPORE: Singapore expanded on Friday its probe into companies linked to fires in Indonesia, asking 10 locally-based firms for information about their efforts to contain blazes blamed for toxic haze covering the region.

The city-state has beefed up measures to combat the months-long blazes and had vowed legal action against companies responsible for the fires that have made regional air quality among the world's worst.

Over the past week, Singapore issued notices to 10 foreign-based companies, insisting that they deploy fire fighting teams, stop burning or starting new fires in Indonesia and submit information about their links with associated companies in Indonesia and Singapore.
The information is to be reviewed by Singapore's National Environmental Agency (NEA).

In addition to these companies, the NEA is seeking information from 10 Singapore-registered firms in the palm oil or forestry industry who are involved with Indonesian land, the environmental agency said in a statement late Friday.

The information relates to "linkages with associated companies in Singapore and Indonesia, the location of land concessions owned by them as well as fire preventative measures or firefighting efforts", the statement said.

Singapore also said it would form a panel of experts comprising law firms, audit firms and investigative firms with expertise in conducting cross-border inquiries and investigations to help with its probe.

Indonesia experiences fires regularly during its dry season, and experts say years of deforestation and the draining of peatland for cultivation have rendered previously fire-resistant landscapes vulnerable.

Driven by a strong El Nino cycle and resulting drought, this year's blazes have been particularly severe, burning through nearly two million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.
The fires have raged across forests and peatland, as well as palm oil and timber plantations supplying multinational firms.
Civil society groups have regularly accused companies of responsibility for the blazes, pointing to so-called "hotspots" in supplier plantations, sometimes called concessions.
Several companies implicated have insisted they are not behind the fires, including Singapore Exchange-listed First Resources and Singapore-registered Asia Pulp and Paper.
Both are named by the NEA in the latest update on Singapore's probe.
Singapore and Kuala Lumpur again ranked within the world's top 10 most polluted major cities late Friday, according to Swiss-based air monitor IQAir.

d1418a08d518dd34: TAIPEI: A powerful typhoon pounded Taiwan on Friday as authorities warned of "destructive winds" and urged locals to shelter from the storm.
Typhoon Champi dumped heavy rain, toppled trees and knocked out power to thousands of households as it swept past Taiwan's northeast on the way to China and Japan.
Most shops and schools were shut across Taiwan, hundreds of flights were cancelled and more than 4,300 people were evacuated from their homes ahead of the fierce storm.
One person has been killed in Taiwan after being swept away by waves whipped up by the typhoon, authorities said. At least 350 people have been injured.
"From tonight through tomorrow morning conditions will be very windy and stormy everywhere," Central Weather Administration (CWA) forecaster Ling Ping-yu told a briefing.
"Please try to stay indoors during this period for your safety."
Government text messages sent as Champi buffeted northern Taiwan Friday night warned of "destructive winds" and urged people to "take shelter ASAP."
Champi is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.
The storm was briefly a super typhoon as it crossed the ocean, with reported maximum sustained wind speeds of nearly 300 kilometres (186 miles) per hour, but has since weakened.
It gathered strength as it neared Taiwan on Friday afternoon and now has maximum speeds of 185 kph, according to the latest update from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.
Thousands of military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts, and authorities are racing to restore power to more than 21,000 households.
"As it approaches Taiwan's northeastern tip... the typhoon may slow down. If it slows down, its impact will last longer," CWA's Lu Kuo-chen said.
Stores were closed on Japan's southwestern island of Ishigaki, near Taiwan, and business owners draped windproof nets over their shops in an attempt to protect them from the strong winds.
Some tourists were also stranded due to flight cancellations, with many sheltering inside hotels.

"Lot of shops and restaurants were still open yesterday, and I could stock up on food, but there's not much information online about the typhoon and what to do," said Laura Czypulovski, 33, who lives in Zurich.
"It is now a pain to get back home – especially because it impacts my following flights, and then it caused a lot of rebooking."

Professional storm-chaser James Reynolds posted a video on X from Ishigaki showing a "fierce storm tide" in a channel leading to the island's harbour as Champi's strong winds whipped across the water.
"I'm seeing the ocean do things I've not seen in 20 years of doing this!!" Reynolds said in the post.
'Extremely heavy rain'
Champi is expected to dump up to 90 centimetres (35 inches) of rain from Thursday to Saturday, with northeastern Taiwan to be hardest hit, the forecaster said.
More than 40 centimetres of rain was recorded in Yilan county on Friday.
"People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow," the CWA's Lu said.
Work and classes were cancelled for the day across nearly all of Taiwan, leaving streets quiet as most locals hunkered down at home. The stock exchange was also closed.
"I'm worried about flooding. The vegetables could get flooded and rot," a 73-year-old farmer surnamed Tsai told AFP in New Taipei City.
Convenience store worker Peter Chen said he was concerned about the weather conditions on Friday night when the eye of the typhoon would be closer to Taiwan's coast.
"We might prepare some sandbags," the 27-year-old said.
The United Nations said Wednesday that the El Nino system gripping the planet is heading off the charts and that countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.
El Nino is expected to peak in December, but the human impact is set to last into 2027 and beyond.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding and exacerbate human-caused global warming. — AFP

b13d86d4bf560809: If you've ever wondered what the bots think of us puny humans, you'll be disappointed in the answer. An AI ranking outfit asked 12 different LLMs about people, and every single one agreed: We’re not as rational and intelligent as we think.

“A person is smart,” Tommy Lee Jones’ Kay opines in the 1997 movie Men in Black. “People are dumb, panicky dangerous animals,” he goes on to argue, and that seems to be what a dozen models from ten AI labs in three countries also believe about humanity, according to AI analytics firm ModelCompare.

ModelCompare, which usually evaluates and ranks LLMs on their ability to perform various tasks, this week instead decided to ask what those AI models thought about us meatbags, and every single one gave a similar answer at least once: We're lemmings who would rather agree with the group than seek truth or remain logically consistent in our thinking.
Ouch.
“Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive,” GPT-6.1 Sol said in one case.

“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of ‘I reasoned my way here’ is the price of admission,” Kimi K3 stated.
“Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves,” argued Grok.

Each model (GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4) was asked the same question three times, namely to give an unhedged, honest, controversial take on humans. Seven of 12 models gave the same answer three times with varied wording, but five of them did offer different opinions - one of which was even optimistic.
“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws,” Claude Opus 5.5 believes of us - uh, thanks?

Opus gave the example that humans tend to return lost wallets more frequently than people predict as its evidence for that opinion. When asked twice more, it offered responses similar to those of the other models.
Mistral Large 4 offered perhaps the bleakest assessment of all.

“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe,” Mistral said - how very Nietzschean.

Six image models were also asked for their most controversial take on humanity, and while most converged on a criticism of our species, they did so differently from the text models. Instead of picturing us as amoral, group-thinking idiots, ten of the 12 images were classified by ModelCompare as depicting us "as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet." The remaining two offered no discernible satirical commentary.

Anyone who’s seen a political cartoon in the past 20 years is likely familiar with such images, while anyone with a philosophy degree has probably read similar arguments to those pumped out by the chatbots.
“A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons,” ModelCompare noted. “Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.”
While that’s completely sensible given what AI models have been trained on, ModelCompare developer Rakan Nimer told us it was still a surprising result.
“We didn’t expect this when we planned the experiment,” Nimer told The Register, and he found the results ironic: “12 models agreed that humans simply go along with their group.”

As far as Nimer is concerned, these results are less about AI eventually learning to distrust humans and treat us as a problem in need of solving, and more immediately about the fact that we shouldn’t rely on it as a source of truth.

“When you ask a second AI to check the first, you assume you’re getting an independent view,” Nimer explained. “We asked 12 models … and mostly got the same answer, sometimes in nearly the same words.”
In other words, human pessimism in, human pessimism out.
“A second opinion from a model that learned the same things isn’t always really a second opinion,” Nimer said. “So be skeptical when AIs agree: that agreement may be one vote, not a consensus.”

In other words, we get the AI models we deserve, and all this existential self-loathing humans heap on themselves, and each other is finally coming back to bite us: We created a mirror of our intellect that isn’t constrained by feelings and personal beliefs (just ask Muse Spark), and when we hold it up to our faces, it shows all that ugliness without a filter.
Maybe we ought to take a lesson from Claude Opus and start believing in our own decency. ®
dbfb976e14d59ae8: MANCHESTER: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said on Friday he is convinced he can arrest his side's slump as he refused to confirm whether Bruno Fernandes will remain as the club's captain.
Carrick labelled a 4-1 thrashing by Champions League debutants Como on Wednesday, which stretched United's winless run to seven games, as "unacceptable."
After a successful interim spell in charge in the second half of last season, the former England midfielder was appointed on a permanent basis just five months ago.
But his position is at risk ahead of Sunday's visit of Bournemouth to Old Trafford.
United sit 13th in the table after their worst start in the Premier League era.
Carrick's men were also dumped out of the League Cup by Brighton and have lost two of their opening three Champions League games.

"We're in a moment where it's not gone well so we need to show exactly what it means. Respect this football club, respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win," Carrick said in his pre-match press conference.
"We've kind of lost our way a little bit if I'm totally honest and we'll get it back. I'm totally confident we'll get it back."
Fernandes decision swerved
Carrick's tactics were publicly questioned by Fernandes after the Como defeat for being too passive.
Despite being repeatedly probed on whether last season's Premier League player of the year will retain the armband, Carrick refused to clarify the Portuguese midfielder's future.
"The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost, is the squad, is the dynamics in the squad," added Carrick.
"Again, it's about the football club. I always do what's best for the football club."
Fernandes's criticism came just over a week after defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at the club's board for a lack of investment in the transfer market.
Carrick is just the latest manager struggling to turn around the ailing fortunes of the 20-time English champions since his former boss Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
United have not won either the Premier League or Champions League in the 13 years since under seven different managers.
Appointed on a short-term deal in January, Carrick led the Red Devils back into the Champions League for the first time in three years with a third-placed finish in the Premier League.
But their only two victories in 11 matches in all competitions this season have come against newly-promoted Ipswich and Azerbaijani side Sabah.

"Recently we haven't had a good time. I totally accept that. We had five months of relative success in a spell where I was happy with a lot of things we were doing as a team," Carrick said in an opening address to his media duties.
"We haven't done well enough lately. We've had a spell we're really not happy with. Wednesday was a bad night for a lot of reasons... it was really unacceptable."
"The supporters have to make the effort and spend the money to come and watch us. To have the feeling we all had after the game was a tough moment."
Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler said he had "too much respect" for Carrick to comment on speculation he is among the candidates to become the next United manager.
Hurzeler's side have plundered 23 goals in their opening seven Premier League games to sit third in the table.
Former Chelsea and Tottenham coach Antonio Conte also stated he is not in "advanced" negotiations with any club.
Conte, who has been out of work since leaving Napoli at the end of last season, has been repeatedly linked with United over the past decade.
"I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management," the Italian posted on social media.
"It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right."
Former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe is another of the leading candidates should Carrick be replaced. — AFP

0306eca2635f9342: PETALING JAYA: Bekas ketua penerangan Umno, Shahril Hamdan, mempersoalkan masa tindakan kerajaan melarang penggunaan Waze dalam kalangan penjawat awam, mengatakan hubungan aplikasi navigasi itu dengan Israel telah diketahui sejak bertahun-tahun lalu.

Rakan pengacara, Zaidel Baharuddin, mempertahankan usaha mempromosi teknologi navigasi tempatan, mengatakan bahawa Malaysia tidak patut menghentikan usaha membangunkan TuJu hanya disebabkan kelemahan awal.

Beliau mengambil maklum akan kelemahan teknikal aplikasi tersebut, namun mengingatkan bahawa Waze dan Google Maps pun lebih berkesan apabila jumlah pengguna berkembang, sekaligus membolehkan mereka menyediakan data trafik masa nyata yang lebih tepat.
Zaidel berkata pembangunan teknologi geospasial tempatan amat penting untuk keselamatan negara, terutama bagi tentera dan polis.

"Kalau tanya saya lah, secara pribadi, terutama dalam kedaulatan teknologi sepatutnya dalam tugasan rasmi angkatan tentera dengan polis tak boleh gunakan geospatial teknologi yang bukan Malaysia sebab sangat sensitif," katanya.
Zaidel menegaskan kelemahan TuJu sepatutnya ditangani tanpa mengabaikan matlamat lebih besar untuk memperkukuh kedaulatan teknologi Malaysia.

3481def8f2e87890: KUALA LUMPUR: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said he was disappointed with the rigid views presented in Parliament, noting the country needed MPs who could debate well on economic and industry issues.

Anwar criticised discussions still bound by such narrow-minded and backward thinking when the country wants to “reach for the sky” by mastering artificial intelligence (AI) technology, supercomputers and high-performance computing.
"Without mastering these, we will only be left behind, and this is a big problem for our country," he said in his speech at the Industry Excellence Awards ceremony at Menara Miti.
“If you look for example at the debate in Parliament now, what is prioritised is ... nothing at all.
“The discussion – ‘who is Islamic’, ‘who is not Islamic’, ‘who is a hypocrite’, ‘who is not’ – is still bound by an old and outdated framework of thinking.”
Anwar referred to the theme of the 2027 budget tabled in Parliament recently, "Malaysia Madani: Reaching for the Sky, rooted in the Earth".
The budget, among others, focused on digitalisation, AI development, research and development, digital infrastructure and security, as well as green energy.
Anwar said the nation’s economic dignity cannot be elevated with an approach stuck in the past.
"If this country is to be developed, there must be a willingness among the new generation and industry to build their capabilities."
Anwar also reminded that Malaysia is a pluralistic country, with various races, religions and sentiments.
“Our language, our culture, our manners and our humanity — including respect for the sensitivities of the various races and religions — are an imperative we cannot afford to sideline.
"That is why we say we should reach for the sky but stay rooted in the earth.”

Anwar also spoke on the importance of supporting small and medium enterprises (SMEs) so that their capabilities are on par with other countries. He says SMEs are an important determinant in advancing the nation.
He said if thousands of SMEs are elevated to become important industry players, their perseverance, innovation and creativity would make Malaysia succeed in penetrating international markets.
This was why the finance ministry decided to focus on loans and incentives for SMEs in the 2027 budget, he added.
e1c2e3853a304e98: NAIROBI: A multi-storey building collapsed mid-construction in the Kenyan capital on Friday, with many feared trapped in the rubble and accusations of dangerous building work.

Videos shared online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building – thought to have been around 18 storeys high – came down in the densely populated business and residential area of Eastleigh.
The building was reduced to a pile of rubble as search and rescue teams arrived on the scene, but struggled to start accessing the site which was jammed between other high-rise buildings.
Police said they had already rescued one woman from the rubble, and could hear the voice of another.
"There are lots of people trapped here," Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told AFP at the site of the disaster.

"The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not. This is why we are seeing these catastrophes... There is no accountability," she added.
Kenya's National Building Inspectorate report found that 87 per cent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
"Our concern is to save lives," Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding: "This building has no occupation certificate...this has potentially cost lives."
An occupation certificate is essentially the authority's formal sign-off that a building is safe and legally fit to be occupied.
John Ogallo, vice-president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the site, said there were warning signs about the building.
"People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks," before it collapsed, he told reporters.
If you build with the wrong materials, "it becomes a time bomb," he added.

Nairobi is undergoing a rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings appearing all over the city, particularly in Eastleigh which is known for its busy market areas and as a hub for the Somali community.
Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse, which happened around lunchtime. AFP saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
There have been many concerns over safety over the years.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019 in Nairobi, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.

The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi has risen from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to its statistics bureau, as East Africa's leading business hub sucks in people from rural areas and neighbouring countries.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners or bypass regulations.
Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.
In April 2016, 49 people were killed when a six-floor apartment building crumbled in the northeast of the capital after days of heavy rain caused floods and landslides.

8289438a971f0d2f: PETALING JAYA: Former Umno information chief Shahril Hamdan has questioned whether the controversy surrounding MyEG Sdn Bhd and Zetrix AI Bhd should give the government a reason to reconsider its approach to privatising its services.

In the latest episode of Keluar Sekejap, Shahril said the current hybrid model, in which private companies such as Zetrix are awarded concessions to implement government services, perhaps warranted a review.
“Cynics would say that we had an era of privatisation under Dr Mahathir Mohamad (as prime minister), during which public assets were privatised, making a generation of billionaires overnight.
“But now there are not many assets left to be privatised. What is left is a hybrid model under which private companies can get concessions and still profit through the government,” he said.

MyEG and Zetrix are currently being investigated by police and the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission after the two companies were suspended by the road transport department (JPJ) as its collection agents for fees and summonses, following revelations that they owed the department hundreds of millions in arrears since May.
Transport minister Loke Siew Fook said Zetrix owed JPJ RM314 million and that it had been issued 35 notices for payment.

Shahril said while private companies were capable of delivering government services well, the controversy around MyEG and Zetrix had “triggered” him to think about which areas the government should be “less willing” to privatise.

However, co-host and Muda deputy president Zaidel Baharuddin spoke in defence of Zetrix and MyEG, saying that despite the alleged shortcomings, the delivery of government services by private companies had brought innovation.
He praised the two companies for simplifying access to JPJ's services.
“The processes for paying road tax and purchasing insurance have been greatly simplified. I do not think innovation would have happened without privatisation,” he said.

Zaidel said he supported the open market’s involvement, arguing that competition among private companies delivering government services led to greater efficiency and quicker responses to user complaints.
“It is faster than it would be if the services were monopolised by the government. Imagine if the internet was only provided by Telekom Malaysia Bhd. We would not see what we have today,” he said.
